concepts.name: Succession Crisis and Weak Post-Ashokan Kings
key_dimensions: Identity and chronology of rulers after Ashoka (Dasharatha, Samprati, Shalishuka, Brihadratha)
Division of empire between Sushima and Kunala — historical debate on partition theory
Contrast between Ashoka's strong centralized rule and fragmented authority of successors
UPSC trap: Dasharatha vs. Ashoka as patron of Barabar Caves — attribution confusion

concepts.name: Assassination of Brihadratha and the Pushyamitra Shunga Coup
key_dimensions: Role of Pushyamitra Shunga as commander-in-chief (Senapati) — nature of the coup
Divyavadana and Puranic sources: conflicting narratives about the event
Significance as transition from Mauryan to Shunga dynasty — political discontinuity
UPSC trap: Whether this was a Brahmanical reaction or a purely military coup — historiographical debate

concepts.name: Theory of Brahmanical Reaction as a Cause of Decline
key_dimensions: H.C. Raychaudhuri's argument: Ashoka's Buddhism alienated the Brahmanical establishment
Counter-argument by Romila Thapar: No evidence of systematic anti-Buddhist persecution by Ashoka
Pushyamitra Shunga's alleged persecution of Buddhists — evidence from Divyavadana vs. archaeological record
UPSC trap: Conflating Ashoka's personal Buddhism with state policy alienating Brahmins — oversimplification trap

concepts.name: Economic Strain and Financial Exhaustion of the Mauryan State
key_dimensions: Cost of maintaining a massive standing army (Pliny's account: 600,000 infantry, 30,000 cavalry, 9,000 elephants)
Ashoka's dhamma policy and charitable expenditures draining the treasury
D.D. Kosambi's argument: Debasing of coinage (punch-marked coins) as evidence of financial crisis
Relationship between agrarian surplus, taxation burden, and peasant resentment

concepts.name: Oppressive Taxation and Agrarian Discontent
key_dimensions: Arthashastra evidence on revenue extraction: bhaga, bali, kara, and hiranya
Megasthenes' account vs. Arthashastra on taxation — corroboration and divergence
Link between over-taxation, peasant flight, and weakening of the agrarian base
UPSC trap: Distinguishing between Arthashastra as prescriptive text vs. actual Mauryan practice

concepts.name: Highly Centralized Administrative Structure and Its Vulnerabilities
key_dimensions: Over-dependence on the personality of the emperor for administrative cohesion
Provincial governors (Kumara/Rajakumara) system — potential for centrifugal tendencies
Arthashastra's elaborate spy system (Guptacharas) as both strength and symptom of fragility
UPSC trap: Centralization as a strength under Chandragupta/Ashoka but a structural weakness for successors

concepts.name: Provincial Rebellions and Centrifugal Forces
key_dimensions: Taxila revolts during Bindusara's reign — early signs of provincial discontent
Kalinga's post-conquest integration challenges despite Ashoka's remorse-driven policy
Emergence of independent kingdoms: Bactrian Greeks in the northwest, Satavahanas in the Deccan
Role of Viceroy Ashoka at Taxila and Ujjain — succession disputes as trigger for rebellion

concepts.name: Foreign Invasions: Indo-Greek (Bactrian Greek) Incursions
key_dimensions: Demetrius I of Bactria's invasion into northwestern India (c. 180 BCE) — timing relative to Mauryan decline
Strabo and Justin as sources for Bactrian Greek expansion into India
Debate: Did invasions cause the decline or exploit an already weakened empire?
UPSC trap: Conflating Indo-Greeks (Yavanas) with earlier Achaemenid/Alexander interactions — chronological trap

concepts.name: Ashoka's Dhamma Policy and Its Political Consequences
key_dimensions: Abolition/reduction of royal hunts and meat consumption — impact on military morale and economy
Non-violence (ahimsa) policy debate: Did it weaken military preparedness?
Romila Thapar's interpretation: Dhamma as political tool, not purely religious — undermining the 'pacifism caused decline' thesis
UPSC trap: Equating Dhamma with Buddhism — Dhamma was a syncretic ethical code, not purely Buddhist

concepts.name: Neglect of the Northwestern Frontier and Military Decline
key_dimensions: Strategic importance of the northwest (Gandhara, Taxila) as gateway to invasions
Evidence of reduced military campaigns post-Kalinga — Ashoka's rock edicts on non-aggression
Comparison with Chandragupta's active military policy in securing the northwest (treaty with Seleucus)
H.C. Raychaudhuri vs. Romila Thapar: Was military decline a cause or a symptom of deeper structural problems?

concepts.name: Rise of the Satavahanas and Southern Fragmentation
key_dimensions: Simuka as founder of Satavahana dynasty — chronological debate (1st century BCE vs. 3rd century BCE)
Satavahana territorial claims overlapping with Mauryan Deccan provinces
Role of Andhra (Satavahana) in Puranic king-lists as successor to Mauryas in the south
UPSC trap: Confusing Satavahanas with Cholas/Pandyas — distinct dynasty with northwestern Deccan base

concepts.name: Fragmentation of the Empire: Eastern and Western Successor States
key_dimensions: Eastern fragment: Shunga dynasty (Magadha core) — continuation of Mauryan administrative legacy
Western fragment: Kanva dynasty succeeding Shungas — brief and weak rule
Kharavela of Kalinga (Hathigumpha inscription) as evidence of Mauryan territorial loss in Odisha
UPSC trap: Assuming Shunga dynasty = complete break — significant administrative and cultural continuity existed

concepts.name: Historiographical Debates on the Primary Cause of Decline
key_dimensions: H.C. Raychaudhuri: Brahmanical reaction + Ashoka's pacifism as primary causes
D.D. Kosambi: Economic/material factors — class contradictions and financial exhaustion
Romila Thapar: Structural weaknesses — over-centralization, succession disputes, economic strain (multi-causal)
UPSC trap: Attributing decline to a single cause — UPSC favors multi-causal, nuanced answers

concepts.name: Role of the Arthashastra in Understanding Mauryan Vulnerabilities
key_dimensions: Arthashastra's elaborate precautions against treachery — evidence of inherent instability concerns
Mandala theory of foreign policy: Explains both Mauryan expansion and vulnerability to peripheral powers
Provisions for dealing with weak/incompetent kings (antardhi) — institutional acknowledgment of succession risks
UPSC trap: Treating Arthashastra as a historical chronicle rather than a prescriptive political treatise

concepts.name: Decline of Trade Networks and Urban Centers
key_dimensions: Mauryan prosperity linked to Uttarapatha and Dakshinapatha trade routes — disruption post-decline
Archaeological evidence: Decline in NBPW (Northern Black Polished Ware) horizon marking end of Mauryan urban phase
Punch-marked coins: Reduced silver content as indicator of economic contraction
UPSC trap: Confusing NBPW decline with PGW (Painted Grey Ware) — different archaeological periods

concepts.name: Buddhist Sources vs. Brahmanical Sources on the Decline
key_dimensions: Divyavadana (Buddhist): Portrays Pushyamitra as anti-Buddhist persecutor — sectarian bias
Puranas (Brahmanical): Frame Shunga takeover as restoration of dharmic order
Ashokavadana narratives: Hagiographic treatment obscuring political realities of late Mauryan period
UPSC trap: Taking either source at face value — both are ideologically colored and require critical triangulation

concepts.name: Kharavela's Hathigumpha Inscription as Evidence of Post-Mauryan Power Vacuum
key_dimensions: Kharavela's campaigns against Magadha — indicating Mauryan successor weakness in the east
Claims of defeating Rajagriha and receiving tribute — reversal of Mauryan dominance over Kalinga
Hathigumpha as a non-Mauryan epigraphic source for the power vacuum — unique evidentiary value
UPSC trap: Dating confusion — Kharavela is 1st century BCE, not immediately post-Ashoka

concepts.name: Impact of Ashoka's Kalinga War on Long-term Mauryan Policy
key_dimensions: Rock Edict XIII: Ashoka's remorse and declaration of dhamma-vijaya over dig-vijaya
Strategic consequences: Abandonment of expansionist military policy after 261 BCE
Debate: Whether Kalinga conquest actually weakened Mauryan resources and triggered chain of problems
UPSC trap: Kalinga War as only a moral turning point — ignoring its strategic and economic implications

concepts.name: Comparison of Mauryan Decline with Other Ancient Empires
key_dimensions: Parallels with Achaemenid decline: Over-extension, succession crises, provincial rebellion
Contrast with Roman Empire's long decline — Mauryan decline was rapid (50 years post-Ashoka)
Lesson of the 'imperial overstretch' theory (Paul Kennedy) applied to Mauryan context
UPSC trap: Over-applying modern political science frameworks to ancient Indian history without contextual grounding
